text: The ticket: a fulfiller reports that SLA breach warnings used to show up on Incidents right away, but lately they're showing up late, sometimes 20 to 30 minutes after they should have. Nothing on the Incident form has changed, and nobody touched any ACL or Business Rule recently. This is a job-performance complaint, worked in order — configuration, then history, then the log, rather than guessing at the script first.

First, identify the real suspect. SLA breach evaluation isn't triggered by a single record edit — it's a sweep-many-records-on-a-timer task, which means the thing to check first is the relevant Scheduled Job, not a Business Rule. Late warnings, rather than missing ones entirely, point toward a timing or performance issue with the job, not a logic error that would make it fail outright.

Before touching the job record, check whether a System Property governs its behavior — many recalculation jobs read a property for how often to run or how large a batch to process per run. If a property controlling the interval or batch size was recently changed, intentionally or by accident, that alone could explain a 20 to 30 minute lag. Check the property's value and its last-updated timestamp — if it changed recently, you may have already found the cause.

If the property checks out, move to the Scheduled Job record itself. Next action tells you when it's due to run next, compared against the interval you'd expect. Then look at the run history: is the job actually firing on schedule, or are the runs themselves taking longer than the gap between them? A job configured to run every 5 minutes that takes 25 minutes to complete each time will back up exactly like this ticket describes, without ever failing outright.

With a specific run's start and end time from the job's history, go to System Log > Errors, or Script Log Statements if the job logs its own progress, and filter to that window — reproduce, then check the timestamp. Look for warnings about volume, like processing far more records than usual, or errors that would cause a retry partway through. A job quietly working through a much larger record set, logged as a warning rather than an error, is a very plausible real cause.

The fix follows whatever the evidence actually shows. A changed property gets restored or deliberately re-tuned. Runs simply taking longer because record volume grew get a scheduling or batch-size adjustment, or a real capacity escalation — not an assumed script rewrite. In every case the order mattered: property, then schedule and history, then log, each step ruling out a cause or handing you the next timestamp to search. Next up: Chapter 7, starting with what an Update Set actually captures.
